outcome: Judged: the status rests on Raymond's 21 September 2026 Zenodo/GitHub bound Λ ≤ 0.149396, an unreviewed AI-assisted computer-assisted bound that supersedes Gomila's 0.1787854 on the same quantity. [Judged 2026-09-28; the researcher's original outcome follows.] The known unconditional upper bound on Λ has been pushed down twice by self-published, non-peer-reviewed computer-assisted works since the frozen revision (0.2 → 0.1787854 by Jude Gomila, July/August 2026; then → 0.149396 by Dale James Raymond, September 2026), both explicitly disclosing AI assistance; neither has been digested by the expert community or appeared on arXiv, and a separate unreviewed preprint claims Λ = 0 outright via a non-standard 'LCK Algebra' framework that shows strong crank hallmarks.

systems: four-agent adversarial AI review panel (unnamed models)

disputes.summary: Three independent, mutually inconsistent-in-status claims exist in the window: Gomila's Λ ≤ 0.1787854 (Jul–Aug 2026, human/AI collaboration, one named real expert reviewer mid-review), Raymond's tighter Λ ≤ 0.149396 (posted to Zenodo/GitHub 21 Sept 2026, explicit 'developed with AI assistance', not peer reviewed, superseding Gomila's numerically but with less external scrutiny so far), and Li Chuankai's claimed exact resolution Λ = 0 (preprints.org, Apr 2026, via a non-standard self-styled 'LCK Algebra'/'holographic extension' framework typical of fringe/crank submissions, also machine-verification-only). None of the three has been digested, published, or even posted to arXiv; only Gomila's has engaged a credentialed subject-matter expert (Dan Romik, UC Davis, author of the standard reference on the Riemann xi function's orthogonal-polynomial theory), and even that engagement is explicitly described as 'in-progress' with the write-up 'not yet peer reviewed.'

summary: Wikipedia's frozen (Jan 2024) statement of Λ's bounds was 0 ≤ Λ ≤ 0.2 (Platt–Trudgian 2020 upper bound, Rodgers–Tao 2018 lower bound); the live Wikipedia article as of my check still reports only these 2018/2020 figures and mentions nothing from the window. Independently, I found real activity: (1) Jude Gomila, a tech entrepreneur (Ultrametric/Golden/Heyzap founder, Cambridge engineering background, not a professional mathematician), self-published a 'computer-assisted proof' on his personal blog and a companion GitHub audit repo lowering the unconditional upper bound on Λ to 0.1787854, discovered 27 July 2026 with a release manuscript dated 20 August 2026. The work explicitly instantiates Polymath 15's Theorem 1.2 at new numerical parameters (Platt–Trudgian's verified RH height, a finite-window barrier certificate, and a tail lemma), and the author states plainly that it was 'developed through human-AI collaboration,' including a 'four-agent adversarial AI review panel' used to stress-test each proof component — but no specific AI systems are named anywhere in the post or repo. Crucially, Dan Romik, a genuine UC Davis mathematician and the author of the standard modern treatment of the Riemann xi function's orthogonal-polynomial expansions, is named as an independent reviewer who 're-proved every analytic lemma' and is reworking the material into 'journal-grade manuscripts' — but the repository itself states this is still 'in-progress' and 'not yet peer reviewed,' and no arXiv posting or journal publication has appeared as of my search (September 2026). This is real, non-trivial expert engagement short of digestion, so I classify it `claimed` rather than `resolved`. (2) A second, even tighter and even less-reviewed claim, Λ ≤ 0.149396 (0.149395073827688 exactly), was deposited to Zenodo by Dale James Raymond on 21 September 2026 (literally the day before my research date), also explicitly 'developed with AI assistance,' also not peer reviewed, and the record itself cautions that 'a successful replay verifies executable finite inequalities; it does not mechanically prove every analytic argument.' (3) A third claim, that Λ = 0 exactly (which would prove the Riemann Hypothesis outright), appears on preprints.org (April 2026) attributed to 'Li Chuankai,' built on a self-styled 'LCK Algebra' extending 'wheel algebra' with a 'universal absorbing element,' invoking 'holographic extension' and 'Gelfand-Naimark-Segal construction' language that is a strong stylistic marker of non-standard/crank mathematics (and plausibly LLM-generated prose); I found no evidence of any mathematician engaging with it, no arXiv posting, and it did not surface in any digestion (Tao's blog, Quanta, MathOverflow). None of these three converge into a stable, expert-endorsed number, and no source I found (Wikipedia's live article, Tao's blog, Quanta) treats any of them as settled. I therefore anchor the `event` on the Gomila claim (July 2026) as the most substantively reviewed of the three, note the newer superseding Raymond claim and the outlying Li Chuankai claim in `disputes`, and set `ai_role` to `assisted` on the basis of Gomila's own account that AI collaboration produced parts of the proof apparatus (with an AI panel used for adversarial review of the mathematics, going beyond mere proofreading) — though I flag real uncertainty about whether this crosses into `generated` for parts of the construction, since the post is vague about exactly which pieces were AI-produced versus human-designed.
competing_reading: If Dan Romik's review, once completed and posted (to arXiv or a journal), confirms the Gomila bound, this would likely become `resolved` on a future check, and a stronger case could be made now that the substantial named-expert engagement already pushes it there. Conversely, one could argue `ai_role` should be `none` if the 'four-agent adversarial AI review panel' is read as only a checking/proofreading step (per §6.2's list of non-qualifying uses) rather than as producing mathematics — the blog post is not fully explicit about which specific lemmas or constructions were AI-authored versus human-authored, so `assisted` is my best reading of an ambiguous disclosure rather than a clean case.
what_would_settle_it: An arXiv posting or journal acceptance of Romik's reworked manuscript, or any digestion of the Gomila/Raymond bounds by a recognized expert venue (Tao's blog, Quanta, a Polymath-style collaborative wiki update, or the Wikipedia article itself being updated) would resolve the status question. A clearer authorial statement of exactly which analytic steps the AI panel produced (versus checked) would resolve the ai_role ambiguity.

judgement.doubts: The status is progress either way: the bullet asks for the value of Λ, and both 2026 results only move the upper bound (F3). The event is switched to Raymond's bound because it is tighter on the same quantity and therefore marks the frontier; Gomila's bound is superseded numerically, although it has had more scrutiny (Romik's review is still in progress). If Raymond's bound fails, the frontier falls back to Gomila's, and the status and AI role stay the same. The AI role is 'assisted' for both bounds, but it rests on thin disclosures (F9). Neither source says which pieces of mathematics the AI produced. Gomila's 'adversarial AI review panel' is only a critic and counts for nothing. Only the 'human–AI collaboration' / 'developed with AI assistance' wording supports 'assisted'. If the sources are read strictly, the role could be 'none'.
